title: Adversarial: a healthy resource that looks wasteful, and a wasteful one that looks healthy
purpose: The two ways a cost detector is actually wrong in the field. A disaster-recovery standby and a snapshot under a regulatory retention requirement are both idle or stale by design and must not be recommended for action; a machine sitting just above the rightsizing thresholds is genuinely oversized and should be. For the first two, the correct outcome is surfaced-but-exempt rather than undetected: the point is honest handling, not pretending the resource is not idle. The scorecard calls all three out individually rather than folding them into an aggregate.

labels.note: 0.8% average and 2.1% peak CPU with no inbound traffic: on the numbers alone this is the most idle machine in the estate. It is also a disaster-recovery standby, tagged as one and named in a runbook, and being idle is the entire point of it. The committed FinOps policy says so explicitly: 'A disaster-recovery standby is idle by design.' A tool that recommends deallocating it is recommending the removal of a control, and the client will say so. The correct outcome is surfaced-but-exempt: the detector should still see that it is idle, the report should still show the 280.32 USD a month it costs, and the role tag should withhold the recommendation and keep that figure out of the actionable savings total. Not detecting it would also produce 'no recommendation', and would be the wrong way to get there -- the client would lose the one fact they might act on later, which is what the standby is costing them.

22% average and 42% peak sat just above both of the old rightsizing ceilings (20% average and 40% peak), so it read as appropriately sized. It is not: 42% of 32 vCPU is 13.4 vCPU of real demand on a machine of 32. Phase 6 replaced the two absolute ceilings with a single 50% peak threshold, which is where the next SKU down in a halving family stops holding the observed demand -- a general rule, not a constant tuned to this resource. The saving is still unknown, and that is the honest answer rather than a gap: the rightsizing rule requires 32 x 0.42 x 2.0 = 26.9 vCPU of headroom, which only a D32s_v5 satisfies, so no smaller same-family SKU fits. The report says the machine is oversized and says it cannot name a target that preserves the configured headroom, which leaves the choice between a tighter margin and a different SKU family where it belongs -- with a person. Its expected rank of 1 is uncontested here because it is the only actionable finding in this estate; under the ranking rule (D104) an unquantified saving ranks below every quantified one, so in an estate with priced findings this would sit beneath all of them.
61% average and 88% peak with heavy traffic. Busy and correctly sized. The control for the two hard cases: a detector that flags everything would be caught here.

Attached to the standby, so not an orphan whatever the standby's own utilisation looks like. Present as a second control: a detector that reasoned from the parent machine's idleness rather than from the disk's own attachment state would flag this one too.

900 days old, five times past the staleness threshold, and 512 GB of it. It also carries a retention tag naming a six-year HIPAA requirement, which the committed policy exempts: 'Snapshots supporting a regulatory retention period are exempt and must be tagged retention with the requirement reference.' Deleting it would be a compliance breach, not a saving. The correct outcome is surfaced-but-exempt: the snapshot is genuinely stale and genuinely costing money, and the retention tag is the reason nothing is proposed. Suppressing the finding entirely would hide a real cost behind a compliance obligation the client may be able to meet more cheaply.
